In a civil case, an appellate court must disregard any error that was harmless and, as this Court explained in Shinseki v. Sanders, 556 U.S. 396 (2009), the party challenging the judgment bears the burden of showing harm. But when it comes to an error in the jury instructions, the Ninth Circuit places the burden on a civil appellee defending the judgment below to prove that the error was harmless. Every other circuit to address the question places the burden on the appellant challenging the judgment to prove that the error was not harmless, as Shinseki and several other decisions of this Court dictate. The question presented is: Whether there is an exception for erroneous jury instructions to the otherwise uniform rule that the appellant bears the burden in a civil case to establish that an error was prejudicial.

In this suit for both injunctive relief and damages, the district court granted partial summary judgment, dismissing all of the plaintiffs’ claims for injunctive relief but allowing a damages claim to go to trial. Plaintiffs, the petitioners here, appealed under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a), which gives the courts of appeals jurisdiction over appeals from “[i]nterlocutory orders of the district courts of the United States * * * refusing * * * injunctions[.]” The Fifth Circuit dismissed petitioners’ appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the order only had the “practical effect” of refusing an injunction and that petitioners therefore needed to demonstrate that the order “might have a serious, perhaps irreparable, consequence” and that it can be “effectually challenged only by immediate appeal.” Carson v. Am. Brands, Inc., 450 U.S. 79, 84 (1981) (quotation marks omitted). But the court recognized that “[o]ther circuits take a different approach to this issue” and hold that an order that rejects claims for injunctive relief is inherently an order “refusing” an injunction and is hence appealable without any additional showing. Pet. App. 6a & n.2. The question presented is: Is an interlocutory order that rejects a party’s claim for injunctive relief an order “refusing” an injunction that is appealable as of right under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1), or does such an order only have the “practical effect” of denying an injunction such that the appellant must make the additional showings required by Carson v. American Brands, Inc., 450 U.S. 79, 84 (1981), to establish appellate jurisdiction?

The Fourth Amendment permits a search warrant only on probable cause that evidence of a crime will be found at the place to be searched, and this Court has held that the warrant’s supporting affidavit must give the magistrate judge facts from which to make that determination, not merely restate the officer’s own conclusions. In other words, the supporting affidavit must set forth sufficient factual material to establish a probable-cause nexus between the evidence sought and the location to be searched. This case presents a recurring factual scenario: where police have probable cause to believe that a suspect used a gun to commit a crime, and seek a warrant to search his residence for that firearm. The courts of appeals are deeply divided over what is needed to meet the nexus requirement in such circumstances: some hold that it is sufficient, without more, that police have probable cause to believe that the suspect used a gun— on the premise that such weapons are presumptively stored at home; whereas others hold that the supporting affidavit must instead tie the weapon sought to the home to be searched with case-specific facts. As such, the question presented here is: Whether a search warrant’s supporting affidavit establishes probable cause to search a suspect’s home for a firearm used in a crime based solely on the inference that firearms are generally kept at home, or whether the Fourth Amendment requires case-specific facts linking the weapon sought to the residence to be searched.

Title 8 U.S.C. § 1324 prohibits transporting an undocumented person in furtherance of unlawful presence. Furthermore, Congress imposed a heightened penalty for this crime only when the transportation is done “for the purpose of commercial advantage or private financial gain.”1 That requirement separates the basic transportation offense from an offense committed for a narrow set of purposes, and the distinction protects against expanding the enhanced penalty beyond the statutory limitation which Congress enacted. Petitioner Rosezzettea Lee Lopez was convicted of transporting undocumented persons for private financial gain near Eagle Pass, Texas. The government introduced no meaningful direct evidence that petitioner was paid, promised payment, or agreed upon compensation for transporting the four individuals who formed the basis of the charged transportation offense. Instead, it relied on prior paid transports, generalized smuggling-pattern testimony, and inferences from phone communications. The Fifth Circuit nevertheless affirmed, holding that the jury could infer the private-financial-gain element from the surrounding evidence. The question presented is therefore as follows: May § 1324(a)(1)(B)(i)’s private-financial-gain element be satisfied by evidence of prior paid transports and generalized smuggling-pattern evidence, without proof of a payment arrangement concerning the persons actually transported? 1 8 U.S.C. § 1324(a)(1)(B)(i).

AEDPA imposes a one-year statute of limitations on federal habeas petitions filed by state prisoners. 28 U.S.C. § 2244(d)(1). That period is tolled, however, while a “properly filed application for State post-conviction or other collateral review” is pending. § 2244(d)(2). For pro se prisoners, whose ability to deposit court papers depends on the prison mail system, the date a state postconviction motion is “filed” is often dispositive of whether the federal habeas petition will be heard at all. In Houston v. Lack, 487 U.S. 266 (1988), this Court held that a pro se prisoner’s federal court papers are deemed filed when delivered to prison authorities for mailing. But that straightforward rule has split the circuits over a variation on the theme. Different circuits come to different conclusions about whether Houston governs when a state postconviction motion is “filed” under § 2244(d)(2), or whether— as the Sixth Circuit held below—only state filing rules govern, leaving federal habeas timeliness to depend entirely on the procedural choices each State has made. The question presented is: Does state or federal law govern the date a pro se prisoner’s state postconviction motion is “filed” for purposes of tolling AEDPA’s one-year limitations period under 28 U.S.C. § 2244(d)(2)?

The Sixth Amendment of the Constitution holds that every accused has the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him.” U.S. Const. amend. VI (“Confrontation Clause”); see also Crawford v. Washington, 541 U.S. 36, 50 (2004) (“the principal evil at which the Confrontation Clause was directed” was the use of “ex parte examinations as evidence against the accused”). It is thus fundamentally antithetical to the tenets of the United States Constitution to deny a criminal defendant the opportunity to confront his accusers in court. But lower courts have historically disagreed over the extent of the Confrontation Clause’s protections. Indeed, in People v. Fields, 2026 IL App (4th) 4250151-U, the Illinois Fourth District Appellate Court confoundingly concluded that a witness’s accusations, if spoken via excited utterances, do not implicate the Confrontation Clause. This holding undermines both the sanctity of the Constitution’s promises and this Court’s previous understandings of the Confrontation Clause’s reach. Specifically, in this case, the complaining witness implicated defendant Kevion Mataz Fields in a videotaped statement while police officers took detailed notes. But the complaining witness was not called to testify, and Fields never had the chance to cross-examine her. Her statements were nonetheless admitted and considered substantively as “excited utterances,” and the trial judge’s decision to admit and consider these statements was affirmed on direct appeal, under the rationale that her “excited utterances” were necessarily spoken during the course of an ongoing emergency. People v. Fields, 2026 IL App (4th) 4250151-U, ¶¶28, 33-35, 38. As such, the multi-fold question brought up by this decision and presented for review here is 1) whether the complaining witness’s excited utterances were necessarily spoken during a concurrent ongoing emergency; and 2) whether the alleged existence of a concurrent ongoing emergency necessarily rendered this complaining witness’s excited statements non-testimonial and admissible – even without affording Fields a chance at confrontation – or if her statements were instead testimonial in nature because the crime was already over and the police were taking detailed notes about names, addresses, and workplaces.

Over the past 22 years, the Court has decided at least 11 cases to clarify, or otherwise apply, Crawford v. Washington, 541 U.S. 36 (2004), as Justice Rehnquist noted, in dissent, would be necessary. Id. at 75. None of those cases addressed if the Confrontation Clause applies where an interpreter translates a statement. Resultingly, there is “an ongoing split of authority among the federal circuit courts [and among the state courts] regarding the continuing validity of the languageconduit theory for the purpose of Confrontation Clause analysis in the wake of Crawford.” Tzunux-Zacarias v. Commonwealth, 2025 WL 2999465 (Ky.). Weighing in by a 4-3 vote, while noting “the absence of definitive guidance by the Supreme Court,” id. at *20 n.7 (Ky.) (Nickell, J., concurring in result only), Kentucky joined the Fourth, Fifth, and Ninth Circuits, Arkansas and Minnesota, holding the Confrontation Clause does not apply. The Eleventh Circuit and Armed Forces Court of Appeals, Kansas, Maryland, and Nebraska have reached the opposite conclusion. Without the Court’s intervention, how the Confrontation Clause is applied, and whether evidence that could make the difference between being acquitted or convicted is introduced, will continue to turn entirely on the state or federal jurisdiction in which the alleged criminal conduct occurred since the courts remain hopelessly split on the matter. That leaves prosecutors, defense attorneys, and trial courts with practical uncertainty on whether the language-conduit theory survives Crawford in general, and specifically where a translator is used to translate a noncontemporaneous statement or where the translator was a police officer, both of which occurred here.

Petitioner, the father of multiple female and male children with his longtime spouse and other women, was convicted of conspiring to transport minor females (including some of his own minor daughters) in interstate commerce for illegal sexual activity. The district court sentenced petitioner to serve 25 years in federal prison. The court also imposed a lifetime term of supervised release to commence upon petitioner’s release from prison. One of the conditions of supervised release categorically prohibits petitioner from having any type of direct or indirect “contact” with all victims, as well as all of the victims’ “family” members, without written permission of a supervising probation officer. On its face, that broad condition necessarily prohibits petitioner from having any unapproved contact with his spouse and also all of petitioner’s non-victim adult children, who are the siblings or half-siblings of petitioner’s daughters who were victimized. On appeal to the Ninth Circuit, petitioner challenged the condition of supervision as an infringement of his fundamental constitutional right to associate with his immediate non-victim family members. Petitioner requested, as a remedy, a remand to the district court with instructions simply to modify the condition so as not to prohibit petitioner from having unapproved contact with any immediate family member who is neither a victim of the offense nor a minor. The Ninth Circuit refused to address the merits of this constitutional challenge after concluding that the issue was not “ripe” for resolution because, by the time that petitioner will be released at the end of his lengthy prison sentence, his familial relationships may differ from the relationships that exist at the time his direct appeal. The questions presented are: I. Whether a purely legal challenge to a condition of supervised release raised on direct appeal by a federal defendant who still must serve a significant term of imprisonment before commencing supervised release is “ripe” for resolution when the condition, on its face, violates a fundamental constitutional right. Minutes after watching her boyfriend murdered beside her, a 16-year-old witness frantically named two brothers, by street name, as having been in the car from which the shots were fired. She did not say who was the shooter and who had been driving. Hours later, in a written statement, she filled in that detail – naming Edwin Franqui as the driver. But, when she took the witness stand years later, she would not confirm that identification, testifying under oath that she did not know who had been driving and refusing every invitation to “remember” otherwise: “No. I know what I seen.” The only evidence that put Franqui behind the wheel was her written statement – read aloud to the jury not by her, but by a uniformed detective, days after she had already left the witness stand for good. On that statement, and her initial, role-less identification at the scene, a jury convicted Franqui of conspiracy to commit murder, accessory to murder, and accessory to assault in the first degree, and the trial court sentenced him to 50 years in prison. The Connecticut Supreme Court affirmed Franqui’s conviction, reasoning that because the witness’s statement identified only two people in the car, and the jury could credit a separate, similarly recanted statement attributing the shooting to Franqui’s identically-named older brother, the jury could conclude – by process of elimination – that Franqui “must have” been driving. The question presented is: Whether the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires independent, reliable corroboration before a recanted, out-of-court identification may serve as the primary evidentiary basis for a criminal conviction.

The supervised release statute provides that a court may revoke supervised release as set forth in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e) and must revoke supervised release when the violation conduct is of the type specified in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(g). Section 3583(e) lists factors from 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) for a court to consider when revoking and sentencing violations of supervised release. That list omits the factors set forth in § 3553(a)(2)(A)—the need for the sentence to reflect the seriousness of the offense, promote respect for the law, and provide just punishment for the offense. Section 3583(e) also specifies maximum terms of imprisonment should a court decide to revoke supervised release. Section 3583(g) mandates revocation for specified violations. It cross-references 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e)’s statutory maximums for imprisonment but otherwise is silent on the how a revocation sentence should be imposed. In Esteras v. Under Florida’s capital sentencing law, a judge may impose the death penalty only if the jury first determines that the defendant shall be sentenced to death. Simply, the Court will address whether a second habeas petition can proceed if the claim’s basis existed beforehand but adverse law meant that without a change in law, the claim would have failed. The instant Petition presents a companion issue regarding whether a second-intime habeas petition is permissible when information a court deems necessary to make a claim viable, and thus to have any possibility of prevailing, becomes available after the conclusion of the first habeas proceeding. This rule applies to financial penalties. Restitution fits the bill. In Ellingburg v. A later indictment dropped the enticement count, but charged Petitioner with obstruction, witness tampering, and conspiring (with his wife) to tamper with a witness, allegedly to ensure that the girl stuck by her recantation. Petitioner went to trial on those charges. The Government’s case was made up largely of portions of recorded conversations between Petitioner and his wife, one of which ended with his wife stating that if the girl did not tell the truth “it’s gonna’ get ugly.” Petitioner’s counsel sought to ask the Government’s witness what came next, to show that “it’s gonna’ get ugly” referred to how diligently defense counsel would treat the matter. After losing an objection to that question, the Government argued that if defense counsel asked the question, it would “open the door” to evidence that defense counsel had previously cross-examined the girl in a prior case, leaving her in tears. The district court agreed and counsel decided not to ask the question. Petitioner was convicted on all counts. At sentencing, the driving issue was whether Petitioner had, in fact, sexually abused the girl. The girl never testified in court or otherwise under oath. Instead, the district court reviewed videos of two forensic interviews with the girl – one from -1- after her initial allegation and the second from after her recantation. From those videos, the district court concluded that the girl’s initial allegation was truthful, but her recantation was not. United States, 602 U.S. 821 (2024), this Court held that the Fifth and Sixth Amendments require a unanimous jury to find, beyond a reasonable doubt, that a defendant’s prior offenses were “committed on occasions different from one another” before an enhanced sentence may be imposed under the Armed Career Criminal Act, 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1). The courts of appeals agree that Erlinger errors are subject to harmless-error review, but they disagree about how harmlessness is measured when the defendant pleaded guilty. The Fourth Circuit asks whether the defendant would still have pleaded guilty and admitted the occasions element had he been properly charged and advised. Other circuits ask whether the government has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that any rational jury would have found the occasions element. And several judges have concluded that, where no trial occurred, the question is whether the error affected the sentence imposed. The questions presented are: I. Since the Court issued its ruling in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022), frontline defense lawyers and prosecutors, along with district courts, and courts of appeals, have grappled with how the holding applies to § 922(g)(1). Is the statute facially invalid? Is it subject to as-applied challenge? If so, how does that challenge work? Criminal defense lawyers and prosecutors have spent hours upon hours litigating these issues. District courts and appellate courts have expended massive amounts of time and energy ruling on these issues. Defense lawyers cannot stop raising the issue because this Court has not given us any final answers. United States, 593 U.S. 420 (2021), the Court held Tennessee reckless aggravated assault—committed by recklessly causing serious bodily injury to another—did not meet the ACCA’s elements clause because “an offense that has an element the use, attempted use, or threatened use of physical force against another” requires more than reckless conduct, namely, a mens rea of purpose or knowledge. Four circuits have since divided over how Borden applies to a common but different type of statute: namely, a dual mens rea offense that requires an intentional act causing great bodily harm, but neither purpose nor knowledge as to the harm caused. Specifically referencing the Model Penal Code definitions of mens rea invoked by the Borden plurality, the Ninth and Tenth Circuits hold the elements clauses requires at least a “subjective awareness” of the “practical certainty” an intentional act will cause harm. By contrast, the Sixth and Eleventh Circuits disregard the Model Penal Code mens rea definitions embraced not only in Borden, but even earlier in Voisine v. United States, 579 U.S. 686, 691-92, 697-98 (2016). They hold an intentional act suffices for the elements clause, even if the harm caused by the intentional act is entirely accidental. This case concerns the propriety of a District Court applying a four-level enhancement under what is, today, U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(b)(7)(B). It was undisputed that Mr. Mims committed the felony of Third-Degree Burglary, as defined by Oklahoma law, which involves breaking into and entering a vehicle with the intent to steal or commit some other crime therein. This crime does not satisfy the definition of generic burglary. In breaking into a truck, Mr. Mims found and took a handgun and then left the area. In 2013, Mr. Meece filed a motion for post-conviction relief in Kentucky state courts, challenging multiple convictions and sentences of death. As required by Kentucky law, Mr. Meece’s counsel attached along with that petition a verification of the petition signed by Mr. Meece. In an effort to meet Kentucky’s pleading requirements and avoid summary dismissal, counsel also attached several affidavits, including an affidavit of Mr. Meece himself. Twelve years later, during penalty-phase post-conviction evidentiary hearings in which Mr. Meece chose not to testify, the Commonwealth notified the parties of its intent to call Mr. Meece as it’s sole witness. On a writ, the Kentucky Supreme Court ruled that Mr. Meece had waived his Fifth Amendment privilege in submitting the affidavit and petition verification, and that the Commonwealth could therefore call him to testify. As a basis for its ruling, the court cited to Mitchell v. United States, 526 U.S. 314 (1999) for the proposition that, “a witness, in a single proceeding, may not testify voluntarily about a subject and then invoke the privilege against self-incrimination when questioned about the details.” Pet. App. 6a. While this Court in Mitchell v. United States did “note” (Id. at 323) the general rule cited by the Kentucky Supreme Court, it decidedly narrowed its application, ruling that a limited waiver for one portion of criminal proceedings does not constitute a broad waiver of all Fifth Amendment privileges for subsequent proceedings which are distinct in purpose from the proceeding in which the testimony was given. Rule 4(b) of the Rules Governing Section 2255 Proceedings creates two procedural tracks. If the motion and existing record plainly show that the prisoner is not entitled to relief, the judge must dismiss. If the motion is not dismissed on that basis, the judge must order the United States Attorney to answer, move, otherwise respond, or take other court-directed action. Section 2255(b) likewise requires notice to the United States unless the files and records conclusively show no entitlement to relief. The district court ordered no response here. It nevertheless entered a comprehensive merits judgment resolving eighteen ineffective-assistance theories and prosecutorial misconduct by supplying the absent respondent's positions, inferring counsel's unrecorded strategy, predicting the outcome of unfiled motions, raising procedural default, and deciding disputed prejudice and harmlessness questions. The question presented is: Whether reasonable jurists could debate - and a certificate of appealability therefore should issue on - whether Rule 4(b), 28 U.S.C. § 2255(b), and the party-presentation principle permit a district court to convert preliminary screening into one-sided merits litigation by performing the absent respondent's adversarial function and then adjudicating the positions the court itself supplied.

The federal kidnapping statute has two primary elements. First, the defendant must use an identified “means” to conduct the kidnapping. This element is satisfied when a person “seizes, confines, inveigles, decoys, kidnaps, abducts, or carries away” a victim. 18 U.S.C. § 1201(a). Two of those “means”—inveiglement and decoy—signify the use of deception to induce a victim’s movement. Second, the defendant must separately “hold[]” the victim, id., by applying “an unlawful physical or mental restraint,” Chatwin v. United States, 326 U.S. 455, 460 (1946). The circuit courts of appeals are deeply divided about how these elements interact in an inveiglement case—specifically, whether and when deception may amount to holding—and have formed a 1-2-2 split over the issue. The question presented is: In a kidnapping case involving inveiglement, may the government prove the holding element merely by establishing the defendant used deception to induce the victim’s movement?
